case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a last-mile delivery driver who transports goods solely within one state is a “transportation worker … engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” under the Federal Arbitration Act’s Section 1 exemption, such that the worker cannot be compelled to arbitrate under the FAA.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. § 1 (the exemption for “contracts of employment of seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Flowers Foods argues that the FAA’s Section 1 exemption should be construed to exclude last-mile delivery drivers who perform only intrastate deliveries to local destinations (e.g., retail stores/consumers). In Flowers’ view, Section 1 covers workers who themselves are actively involved in interstate transportation (crossing state lines or being part of a continuous interstate transportation function in a narrower sense), and extending the exemption to intrastate last-mile drivers would create administrability problems and uncertain, fact-heavy line drawing about where an “interstate journey” begins and ends. Flowers also points to the Tenth Circuit’s multi-factor approach as overly complicated and contends that a clearer rule is needed to preserve the FAA’s pro-arbitration framework and avoid turning routine distribution work into ‘interstate commerce’ for FAA-exemption purposes.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Brock argues that Section 1 turns on whether the worker is part of the practical movement of goods in interstate commerce, not on whether the worker personally crosses state lines. Because the goods Brock delivers have traveled interstate and his deliveries complete a single, continuous stream of interstate commerce (a relay that continues until the goods are delivered to their intended destination), he falls within the ‘class of workers’ engaged in interstate commerce. Brock further contends that historical (including pre-1925) interstate-commerce and shipment-continuity principles show that intrastate legs can still be interstate commerce when they are part of an interstate shipment’s continuous journey, and that the correct legal answer is not an automatic exclusion for last-mile drivers but a context-sensitive inquiry into whether the shipment’s interstate journey had ended (e.g., at a warehouse/wholesaler) before the worker transported the goods.
key_precedents: United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007)
Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.)
Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon, 596 U.S. 450 (2022)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point: that an intrastate leg may still be part of a “continuous interstate journey,” and under Saxon the last-mile drivers could be a “direct and necessary” link in moving goods. But Circuit City’s insistence on a narrow §1 carveout, read with ejusdem generis, makes it hard to treat local in-state delivery from an in-state facility as the sort of “engaged in … interstate commerce” work exemplified by seamen and railroad employees, especially when the proposed continuity/intent test turns §1 on fact-bound determinations about when goods have ‘come to rest.’ Saxon does not compel that result; it directs us to the class’s “actual work,” and a class defined by purely intrastate distribution is meaningfully different from classes whose occupation is interstate carriage itself. Justice Barrett’s reliance on stipulated “interstate relay” characterizations underscores the administrability concern Justice Alito raises: if labels about supply-chain continuity control, the exemption risks expanding with modern logistics beyond what Congress clearly carved out in §1.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s proposed “continuous interstate journey” test is the strongest counterargument, but I cannot locate it in the text of §1 as originally understood; it imports an atextual continuity/intent inquiry (when goods ‘come to rest,’ whose intent controls) that resembles regulatory stream-of-commerce doctrines rather than the FAA’s narrow carveout. Under Circuit City’s ejusdem generis framework, the residual clause must be read in light of “seamen” and “railroad employees,” i.e., classes whose occupation is interstate transportation itself, not local in-state distribution from an in-state facility, even if the goods earlier moved across state lines. Justice Barrett’s reliance on the stipulated “interstate relay” label does not cure that defect, because allowing supply-chain characterizations to control risks collapsing §1 into a broad exemption for modern logistics that Congress did not clearly enact. Administrability concerns raised by the Chief Justice and Justice Alito do not drive my conclusion, but they confirm that respondents’ approach untethers §1 from a stable, text-bound meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor’s “continuous interstate journey” proposal is the most serious counter, but it effectively imports a stream-of-commerce/through-shipment inquiry into FAA §1 that the text does not supply and that Circuit City cautions us to avoid by reading the residual clause narrowly under ejusdem generis. Justice Barrett’s reliance on the stipulated “interstate relay” label illustrates the administrability problem: if characterization of supply-chain continuity controls, then vast categories of intrastate delivery workers become “interstate” whenever goods originated out of state, threatening to swallow the FAA’s general rule. Saxon’s duties-based framing helps identify the relevant class of workers, but it does not erase §1’s limiting phrase “engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” as that phrase would have been understood in 1925—aimed at workers whose occupation is interstate carriage akin to seamen and railroad employees, not in-state delivery from an in-state facility to in-state customers. Because the opposing approach turns §1 on fact-bound disputes about intent and when goods have ‘come to rest,’ I do not think it is consistent with a textual, administrable reading of the carveout Congress enacted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan raise the strongest point: that a “continuous journey/intent” inquiry could become fact-bound and hard to administer, potentially stretching Circuit City’s narrow construction. But that concern cannot justify reading into §1 a categorical intrastate-delivery exclusion that the text does not supply and that Saxon’s duties-focused framework rejects; as Justice Gorsuch explains, the limiting principle comes from whether the class’s work is a direct and necessary leg of interstate transportation, not from whether an individual crosses a border. Justice Thomas’s insistence that the occupation be interstate carriage “itself” effectively reintroduces a border-crossing proxy Saxon disclaimed and underreads “engaged in … interstate commerce” in a modern relay-based system. The administrability problem is real, but the answer is to require objective indicia of a through-shipment (as Justice Barrett suggests), not to rewrite §1 in a way that leaves vulnerable last-mile transportation workers compelled into arbitration despite performing core interstate-movement work on these stipulated facts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor make the best case that an intrastate leg can still be part of one interstate movement, and Saxon’s “direct and necessary role” language could be read to accommodate that. But I remain persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s point that the proposed “continuous journey/intent” approach lacks a clear textual hook in §1’s residual clause and would turn Circuit City’s narrow carveout into a logistics-intensive inquiry about when goods have ‘come to rest’ and whose intent controls. Under Saxon, we define the class by what these workers actually do; a class defined by in-state deliveries from an in-state facility to in-state customers is not obviously of the same kind as “seamen” and “railroad employees” engaged in interstate transportation as such, and I do not see a workable limiting principle in respondents’ framing that keeps the exemption coherently cabined. Justice Barrett’s suggestion of using “objective indicia” of through-shipment helps, but it still feels like importing a regulatory continuity test rather than applying the statutory text as constrained by ejusdem generis and Circuit City.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan make the strongest point about administrability: a “continuous journey/intent” inquiry can devolve into disputes about logistics and when goods have “come to rest.” But that concern cannot justify reading an extra-textual categorical rule into §1 that excludes all intrastate last‑mile delivery, especially after Saxon’s instruction to focus on the class of workers’ actual duties and whether they play a “direct and necessary role” in moving goods in interstate commerce. Justice Thomas’s approach, tying §1 largely to workers who themselves perform border-crossing carriage, effectively rewrites “engaged in … interstate commerce” to mean “personally crossing state lines,” a rigidity Saxon rejected. Circuit City’s narrow-construction principle is still satisfied by confining §1 to transportation workers completing an interstate relay to a specific destination (as Justice Barrett emphasizes), as opposed to local distribution of goods that have come to rest as general inventory.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor are right that Saxon rejects a rigid state-line-crossing requirement and that an intrastate “last mile” can be a necessary leg of an interstate movement. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts (and Justices Kagan and Alito) that respondents’ proposed “continuous journey/intent/come-to-rest” framework is not well moored to FAA §1’s text as narrowed by Circuit City’s ejusdem generis reading; it risks turning the exemption into a fact-bound shipping-logistics inquiry rather than an inquiry into whether the class of workers is of the same kind as seamen and railroad employees whose occupation is interstate carriage itself. Even accepting Justice Barrett’s point about objective indicia of through-shipment, the stipulated “interstate relay” label underscores the administrability and expansion problem: modern supply chains could characterize vast swaths of local distribution as interstate, effectively diluting Circuit City’s narrow carveout. On this record, the class here—drivers making in-state deliveries from an in-state facility to in-state endpoints—remains meaningfully unlike the historically understood categories Congress singled out, so I would continue to enforce the arbitration agreement under the FAA.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability objection is the strongest point for Petitioner, but I do not think it justifies reading an extra-textual, categorical intrastate-delivery exclusion into §1’s phrase “engaged in … interstate commerce.” Circuit City’s instruction to construe the residual clause narrowly constrains §1 to transportation workers akin to seamen and railroad employees, yet Saxon supplies the operative method—looking to the class’s actual duties and whether they play a “direct and necessary role” in the interstate movement of goods—without imposing a border-crossing requirement or a warehouse-stop safe harbor. Justice Thomas is right to worry about a free-floating stream-of-commerce rule, but that concern can be answered by requiring objective evidence of a through-shipment to a specific destination (not merely out-of-state origin), rather than by rewriting the statute to exclude all last-mile work. On the stipulated record describing a single interstate relay to intended endpoints, the class’s work remains sufficiently tied to the practical interstate carriage to fall within §1 as originally understood, so I do not see a legal basis to change my vote.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest point for Petitioner—pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan—is administrability: a “continuous journey/intent” inquiry could become a logistics-heavy, fact-bound exercise that risks diluting Circuit City’s instruction to construe §1 narrowly. But that concern does not justify a categorical intrastate-delivery carveout that the text does not supply and that Saxon’s duties-focused framework rejects; instead, as Justice Barrett suggests, courts can require objective indicia that the class’s work is the final, direct, and necessary leg of a single through-shipment to a specific destination, rather than delivery from goods that have come to rest as general inventory. Justice Thomas’s proposed border-crossing emphasis would effectively reinstate the rigid crossing requirement Saxon disclaimed and underread “engaged in … interstate commerce” in modern relay-based transportation. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, a workable limiting principle that tracks actual job functions and practical consequences is preferable to rewriting §1 to force arbitration on workers performing core interstate-transportation work simply because their segment is intrastate.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1’s residual clause must be read narrowly under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams, and by ejusdem generis it targets classes of workers akin to seamen and railroad employees—workers whose “actual work” is the direct interstate transportation of goods. Under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon, the focus is on the class of workers’ duties, not merely that the goods previously traveled in interstate commerce; an intrastate last-mile driver delivering from an in-state facility to in-state destinations is not necessarily performing interstate transportation. Given the administrability and line-drawing concerns reflected in the record, the narrower, precedent-consistent resolution is that purely intrastate last-mile delivery work, without more, does not fall within §1’s “engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” exemption. The FAA therefore applies, and the worker may be compelled to arbitrate absent another valid basis to resist enforcement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAA’s §1 exemption covers “seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under ejusdem generis that residual clause must be limited to classes of workers similar to seamen and railroad employees—i.e., those who themselves perform interstate transportation work. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams held §1 is a narrow carveout confined to transportation workers “engaged in commerce” in the 1925 sense, and Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon instructs the inquiry focuses on what the worker does, not the employer’s general business. A last-mile driver who transports goods solely intrastate to local destinations is not “engaged in … interstate commerce” in the requisite way because his work is intrastate distribution rather than interstate carriage. Extending §1 to all intrastate delivery of previously interstate goods would untether the text from its original public meaning and improperly expand the exemption beyond Congress’s narrow enumeration in §1.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only “seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under ejusdem generis that residual phrase should be read narrowly to reach workers who are themselves part of the interstate transportation industry, not every intrastate distributor of goods that once crossed state lines. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams instructs that the §1 exemption receives a “narrow construction” and “precise reading,” which counsels against an administratively unworkable, fact-intensive ‘stream of commerce’ test that would turn routine local deliveries into ‘interstate commerce’ for FAA purposes. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon focuses on the “actual work” performed by the class of workers, but it does not require treating purely intrastate last-mile deliveries to local retail endpoints as engagement in interstate commerce whenever the goods earlier moved across state lines; extending §1 that far would swallow much of the FAA in modern logistics. Because Brock’s work is confined within one State and does not itself constitute interstate transportation in the ordinary 1925 sense, the arbitration agreement is enforceable under the FAA.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FAA §1 exempts “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon the inquiry focuses on the worker’s actual duties and whether that class plays a direct and necessary role in the interstate movement of goods. A last-mile delivery driver who completes the final leg of a continuous interstate shipment can be “actively engaged in transportation” in the channels of interstate commerce even if he never crosses state lines, because his work is part of the same interstate relay that delivers goods to their intended destination. Flowers’ proposed categorical exclusion for all intrastate last-mile drivers would undercut §1’s protective function for transportation workers and permit compelled arbitration precisely where workers have the least bargaining power and greatest need for access to court. Administrability concerns can be handled case-by-case by asking whether the interstate journey had ended (e.g., goods warehoused for local redistribution) before the driver’s work, rather than adopting an across-the-board rule that forecloses the exemption.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only “seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Circuit City the residual clause gets a “narrow construction” and is limited by ejusdem generis to transportation workers whose work is closely tied to interstate transportation in the way those enumerated categories are. Saxon instructs that we identify the relevant “class of workers” by the workers’ “actual work,” not simply by the interstate origin of the goods; a last-mile driver who transports goods solely within one State, after they have come to rest in local distribution, is not ordinarily “engaged in” interstate commerce in the Section 1 sense. Because respondent’s proposed “continuous journey/intent” test invites fact-intensive line drawing about when an interstate journey ends—precisely the administrability concerns flagged at argument—it risks expanding Section 1 beyond its textually cabined function and undermining the FAA’s coherent, workable pro-arbitration framework. On this record, the better reading is that purely intrastate last-mile delivery is not categorically within the FAA § 1 exemption.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Circuit City that residual clause must be read narrowly by ejusdem generis with “seamen” and “railroad employees,” i.e., workers whose occupation is transportation in the channels of interstate commerce. Applying Saxon’s two-step framework, the relevant class here is last-mile delivery drivers who transport goods, and a class is “engaged in … interstate commerce” when it plays a “direct and necessary role” in the interstate movement of goods, even if the worker does not personally cross state lines. Where, as alleged, the intrastate leg is part of a single continuous interstate journey of the goods (not goods that have come to rest for local disposition), that class is engaged in interstate commerce within § 1 and cannot be compelled to arbitrate under the FAA. The administrability concerns cannot override the statutory text and the historical understanding that intrastate legs can remain interstate commerce when they complete an interstate shipment’s continuous movement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: FAA § 1’s residual clause must be read narrowly under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams, applying ejusdem generis to limit “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” to workers whose actual work is akin to seamen and railroad employees—i.e., those directly involved in the interstate transportation of goods. Under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon, the focus is on the “class of workers” and the tasks they perform, not simply that the goods once moved interstate; a last-mile driver making purely intrastate deliveries to local destinations is not, by virtue of that intrastate work alone, engaged in interstate commerce in the Section 1 sense. Extending the exemption to intrastate last-mile distribution would invite the administrability and line-drawing problems highlighted at argument (e.g., intent and where the interstate journey ends), undermining the FAA’s predictable, pro-arbitration framework and exceeding the limited carveout Congress adopted in § 1. Accordingly, Brock may not invoke § 1’s exemption on the stipulated facts and can be compelled to arbitrate under the FAA.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: FAA §1 exempts “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams that residual clause is read narrowly via ejusdem generis to cover transportation workers akin to seamen and railroad employees. But Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon directs that we identify the relevant “class of workers” by the worker’s “actual work,” and it rejects a rigid requirement that the worker personally cross state lines; the question is whether the class is actively engaged in the interstate transportation of goods. Where a last-mile driver’s intrastate deliveries are a leg of a single, continuous interstate shipment to its intended destination, that driver is part of the practical interstate movement of goods and thus falls within §1’s transportation-worker exemption. Because the stipulated facts here frame Brock’s work as completing that interstate relay, he cannot be compelled to arbitrate under the FAA.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1 of the FAA exempts “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon the inquiry focuses on the class’s “actual work,” not a categorical requirement that the worker personally cross state lines. If Brock’s last-mile deliveries are the final leg of a continuous interstate journey of goods shipped with an intended destination beyond the in-state warehouse, then his class of workers is engaged in interstate commerce within the meaning of 9 U.S.C. § 1 even though the driving is intrastate. Flowers’ proposed bright-line exclusion for all last-mile intrastate drivers is inconsistent with Saxon’s functional approach and risks procedural unfairness by compelling arbitration where workers are performing an integral interstate-transportation function. Administrability concerns can be addressed through a fact-sensitive continuity-of-shipment inquiry rather than rewriting the exemption to turn solely on border-crossing.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether “last-mile” delivery drivers who transport goods solely within one state are excluded from the Federal Arbitration Act under the Section 1 exemption for “contracts of employment” of workers engaged in interstate commerce.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. § 1 (the transportation-worker exemption for “contracts of employment of seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Flowers Foods, et al.) argue that the FAA’s Section 1 exemption should be applied narrowly and generally does not cover last-mile delivery drivers who make purely intrastate deliveries to retail customers or local endpoints. In their view, once goods have reached a local warehouse/distribution point and are later delivered intrastate, that final leg is not “interstate commerce” for Section 1 purposes, so arbitration agreements remain enforceable under the FAA. Petitioners also emphasize administrability concerns, contending that respondent’s approach forces courts into difficult, fact-intensive line-drawing about the structure of modern distribution chains and the subjective or commercial ‘intent’ behind shipments.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Brock) argues that last-mile drivers can fall within Section 1 when their work is part of the continuous interstate movement of goods—i.e., when the goods they deliver have been shipped across state lines as part of a single integrated journey and the intrastate delivery is merely a final leg of that interstate transportation. Respondent resists an automatic rule that the interstate journey necessarily ends at a warehouse or wholesaler, and contends the correct inquiry (consistent with older commerce/transportation cases referenced at argument) turns on whether, at the time of shipment, the goods were destined as part of a continuous interstate movement to their ultimate endpoint (not simply the abstract fact that consumers are the ultimate purchasers). Respondent acknowledges the answer can be ‘it depends,’ but maintains courts can resolve most cases without unworkable line-drawing and that categorical exclusion of last-mile drivers is inconsistent with the statutory text and the historical understanding of interstate transportation.
key_precedents: United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007)
Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.)
Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon, 596 U.S. 450 (2022)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that neither §1’s text nor Saxon imposes a border-crossing or warehouse “come to rest” rule, and that historical “practical continuity of movement” doctrine sometimes treated intrastate legs as interstate commerce. But as Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh stress, importing that doctrine here risks converting §1 into a shipment-intent/flow-of-goods inquiry that is fact-intensive and hard to cabin, which sits uneasily with Circuit City’s instruction to construe the residual clause narrowly and with the FAA’s general pro-enforcement structure. Saxon’s worker-focused approach cuts the other way for this class: if their ordinary duties are local, last-mile deliveries from an in-state facility to in-state customers, that is not sufficiently analogous to seamen and railroad employees to justify extending the exemption whenever goods previously traveled interstate. I remain open to a narrower rule that captures workers more directly participating in interstate carriage, but I am not persuaded the respondents’ “integrated shipment” theory supplies an administrable, precedent-consistent boundary here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s administrability concerns are the strongest counterpoint, but they cannot justify a categorical “warehouse/come-to-rest” or border-crossing limitation that §1 does not contain. Circuit City’s instruction to read the residual clause narrowly operates through ejusdem generis—confining the exemption to transportation workers analogous to seamen and railroad employees—not by rewriting the meaning of “engaged in … interstate commerce” to exclude intrastate legs that are part of a single, practically continuous interstate movement. Saxon, as Justice Barrett emphasizes, properly keeps the inquiry worker- and class-focused (what duties the class performs in moving goods in commerce), which supplies a textual limiting principle and answers Justice Gorsuch’s fear of a boundless goods-centered test. Because the petitioners’ bright line would add an atextual cutoff and underinclude transportation workers who complete an integrated interstate shipment, it does not overcome the original public meaning of the statutory text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that “practical continuity of movement” has historical roots and §1 does not expressly require border-crossing or make a warehouse stop dispositive. But their approach still shifts the statutory focus from the “class of workers” and what that class does to a goods-and-logistics inquiry (predetermined endpoints, shipper intent, integrated flows) that Circuit City warned against when it insisted the residual clause be read narrowly by ejusdem generis. Justice Thomas’s reassurance that courts can keep it “worker-focused” does not solve the administrability problem Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh identify, because determining whether these local deliveries are part of an “ongoing interstate stream” necessarily invites litigation over upstream commercial arrangements rather than the workers’ ordinary duties. Under Saxon’s duty-centered framing, a class performing only intrastate last-mile deliveries from an in-state facility to in-state customers is not, in ordinary 1925 usage comparable to seamen and railroad employees, “engaged in interstate commerce” as §1 uses that phrase.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and the Chief Justice’s administrability concern is the strongest point for petitioner, because a free-ranging “shipper intent” test could devolve into goods-focused mini-trials and threaten Circuit City’s instruction to construe §1 narrowly. But Saxon, as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett stress, already supplies the needed constraint: we define the class by what the workers do, and ask whether their ordinary duties directly move goods as part of an ongoing interstate stream—without adding an atextual “goods come to rest at the warehouse” cutoff. Properly framed, the inquiry turns on regular logistics practices (predetermined endpoints and integrated routing) rather than speculative intent, which answers Justice Kavanaugh’s indeterminacy objection while preserving §1’s transportation-worker core. Because petitioners’ categorical intrastate-last-mile exclusion would underinclude workers who in practical reality complete interstate carriage and would further entrench forced arbitration for vulnerable workers, I remain with respondent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito are right to flag administrability: a free-ranging “continuous journey/intent” test could devolve into speculative inquiry about upstream logistics, in tension with Circuit City’s instruction to keep §1 narrow. But I do not think that justifies Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s categorical rule that interstate commerce effectively ends at an in-state warehouse for all last-mile drivers, because that adds a warehouse “come to rest” cutoff not found in the text and conflicts with Saxon’s worker-centered approach. The workable middle ground is Saxon’s limiting principle: define the class by actual duties and ask whether those duties play a direct and necessary role in moving goods in interstate commerce as part of the employer’s regular, integrated interstate flow to predetermined endpoints—an inquiry that can be applied without turning every case into a broad shipping-intent trial. On that framing, §1 remains narrow (transportation-worker analogues to seamen/railroad employees) without rewriting “interstate commerce” to exclude intrastate legs that complete an ongoing interstate movement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that neither border-crossing nor a warehouse stop is textually dispositive, and that contemporaneous “practical continuity of movement” doctrine can treat an intrastate leg as interstate commerce. But even accepting that history, her approach still pivots §1 from a worker-and-class inquiry to a shipment-design inquiry—asking whether goods remain in an “interstate stream” based on upstream logistics—inviting the administrability and boundlessness concerns Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito identify, and doing so without a clear textual stopping point. Under Circuit City’s ejusdem generis instruction and Saxon’s insistence on defining the relevant “class of workers” by their duties, a class that performs only local, in-state last-mile deliveries to in-state customers is not, in the 1925 sense, “engaged in interstate commerce” akin to seamen and railroad employees merely because the items once moved across state lines. I therefore stay with petitioner, while agreeing with Justice Thomas that cases involving classes of workers who themselves perform cross-border carriage (or its functional equivalent) may fall on the other side under Saxon.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas make the respondent’s strongest point: historical “practical continuity of movement” can treat an intrastate leg as part of interstate commerce, and Saxon does not impose a border-crossing requirement. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito that respondent’s proposed continuity/intent framework risks converting §1 into a goods-and-logistics inquiry with indeterminate bounds, in tension with Circuit City’s narrow ejusdem generis approach and the FAA’s background rule of enforceability. Saxon’s worker-centered method, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, counsels defining the class by what it does; a class performing only in-state last-mile deliveries from an in-state facility is not, in the ordinary 1925 sense, “engaged in interstate commerce” akin to seamen and railroad employees, even if the goods earlier traveled interstate. I would preserve a more administrable, duty-based limitation while leaving room for cases where the class more directly participates in interstate carriage (e.g., cross-border routes or functional equivalents).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is administrability: a “continuous journey/shipper intent” inquiry could devolve into litigating upstream logistics and thereby dilute Circuit City’s instruction to construe §1 narrowly. But that concern does not justify their categorical rule that purely intrastate last-mile drivers are generally outside §1, because the statutory text contains no border-crossing requirement and does not make an in-state warehouse stop dispositive; adding either would be atextual. As Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan emphasize, Saxon supplies the limiting principle by keeping the inquiry worker- and class-centered: whether this class of transportation workers, in the ordinary course, directly moves goods as a leg of interstate commerce (including a practically continuous interstate flow to predetermined endpoints). On that approach, “narrowly” under Circuit City is satisfied by restricting §1 to transportation-worker classes analogous to seamen and railroad employees, without importing a “come to rest” cutoff that risks underinclusion inconsistent with the original public meaning of “interstate commerce.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is administrability: a “continuous journey/shipper intent” test can devolve into goods-focused, fact-bound litigation and risk pushing §1 beyond Circuit City’s transportation-worker core. But Saxon already commits us to a worker-duty inquiry, and—as Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor emphasize—we can keep the analysis cabined by asking whether this class of drivers, as a regular part of its job, performs the final leg of an arranged interstate shipment to predetermined endpoints, rather than adjudicating amorphous upstream “intent.” That framing avoids an atextual “warehouse come-to-rest” cutoff and better tracks the practical consequences of integrated logistics in modern commerce without letting §1 swallow §2. Because the petitioners’ categorical intrastate-last-mile exclusion would underinclude transportation workers who functionally complete interstate carriage, I remain with respondent.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1 of the FAA is an exemption that our precedents instruct must be read narrowly and with attention to the kind of transportation work Congress had in mind—“seamen” and “railroad employees”—under ejusdem generis. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams requires a “narrow construction” of the residual clause, and Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon directs courts to define the relevant “class of workers” by the “actual work” they perform, i.e., whether they are themselves engaged in interstate transportation. Where drivers’ work is solely intrastate “last-mile” delivery from an in-state warehouse to in-state destinations, treating them categorically as “engaged in interstate commerce” would expand the exemption beyond its historically circumscribed scope and invite the administrability problems highlighted at argument. A narrow holding that purely intrastate last-mile drivers are not within § 1 preserves the FAA’s core rule of enforceability while leaving for future cases any fact pattern involving drivers who themselves cross state lines or are tightly integrated with interstate carriage.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “contracts of employment of seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under ejusdem generis the residual clause reaches transportation workers similar in kind to seamen and railroad employees. The original public meaning of being “engaged in interstate commerce” in 1925 included workers who handled goods moving in a continuous interstate journey, even where a particular leg occurred wholly within one State, so long as the intrastate leg was practically part of the interstate transportation. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon instructs that the inquiry turns on what the worker does—whether the worker’s duties are part of the movement of goods in interstate commerce—not on formalities like where title passes or an administrability-based categorical cutoff at a warehouse. Because last-mile drivers can be part of that continuous interstate movement, there is no automatic rule excluding them from § 1, and the exemption may apply on the facts here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1 of the FAA exempts only “contracts of employment of seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams that residual clause must be read narrowly (ejusdem generis) to cover only transportation workers actually engaged in interstate commerce. A driver who performs deliveries wholly within one State after goods have come to rest at an in-state warehouse is not, by virtue of that intrastate leg alone, “engaged in” interstate commerce within the meaning that term carried in 1925, and expanding the exemption would risk swallowing the FAA’s pro-arbitration rule in § 2. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon reinforces that the inquiry focuses on what the worker does, but it does not require treating every intrastate delivery of previously shipped goods as interstate commerce, particularly when that approach yields the kind of administrability problems and indeterminate “intent” inquiries highlighted at argument. The better textual and practical reading is a clearer rule that last-mile intrastate delivery, standing alone, does not trigger § 1’s narrow exemption, leaving the arbitration agreement enforceable under the FAA.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FAA §1 exempts “contracts of employment” of a “class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and the text does not impose an automatic rule that interstate commerce ends the moment goods pause at an in-state warehouse. Under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon, the inquiry is functional and focuses on the worker’s actual duties and whether, as a practical matter, they are part of the interstate transportation of goods—work that can include intrastate segments that complete a continuous interstate movement. A categorical exclusion of last-mile drivers would both depart from that practical-work framework and risk compelling arbitration against lower-wage transportation workers who may have limited bargaining power, undermining access to court remedies. I would therefore reject petitioners’ per se rule and hold that last-mile drivers are exempt when their deliveries are a final leg of a continuous interstate journey of goods, leaving more detailed line-drawing to fact-bound applications.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “contracts of employment” of “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams that residual clause is read narrowly by ejusdem generis but still covers transportation workers who perform a direct part of interstate carriage. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon directs courts to define the relevant “class of workers” by the workers’ actual job duties and asks whether they “play a direct and necessary role in the free flow of goods across borders,” which can be true even when the worker’s own trips are intrastate if they are a final leg in a continuous interstate movement of goods. A categorical rule that the interstate journey always ends at a warehouse is hard to square with that text-focused, function-based approach and risks underinclusion where the shipment is arranged from the outset as an integrated interstate delivery to local endpoints. While administrability concerns are real, they can be managed by a limited inquiry into whether the employer’s delivery work is part of an ongoing interstate flow (rather than an automatic exclusion), preserving statutory coherence with § 1’s transportation-worker focus.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only "contracts of employment" of "seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce," and under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams that residual clause receives a "narrow" reading informed by ejusdem generis. Applying Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon, the question turns on the "actual work" performed by the relevant class of workers; drivers who make deliveries wholly within a single State to local endpoints are not themselves engaged in interstate commerce in the ordinary 1925 sense, even if the goods earlier crossed state lines. Adopting respondent’s continuous-journey/intent test risks collapsing the exemption into a goods-focused inquiry that would sweep in many purely local workers (warehouse, retail handling) and invites indeterminate, fact-intensive line-drawing inconsistent with the FAA’s text and administrable boundaries. Where Congress has not clearly displaced the FAA’s command to enforce arbitration agreements, we should not expand an exemption beyond its plain, historically cabined meaning.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1 of the FAA exempts only “seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams that residual clause receives a narrow, ejusdem generis construction tied to transportation workers who themselves are engaged in interstate commerce. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon directs courts to define the relevant “class of workers” by the actual work they perform and asks whether that work involves active, direct participation in the interstate transportation of goods; drivers making deliveries wholly within one State after goods have arrived at a local distribution point are not, as a class, engaged in interstate commerce in the way Section 1 contemplates. A broader “continuous flow/intent of shipment” test would invite the kind of fact-intensive, difficult line-drawing and reduced administrability highlighted at argument, undermining the FAA’s workability and predictable enforcement of arbitration agreements. Consistent with precedent, history, and practical workability, the better rule is that purely intrastate last-mile delivery drivers are not categorically within the Section 1 exemption.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “contracts of employment” of “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under the ordinary public meaning in 1925, goods could remain in interstate commerce through an intrastate “last leg” when that leg is part of a continuous interstate movement to an intended endpoint. That historical understanding is reflected in contemporaneous sources and transportation cases recognizing a “practical continuity of movement,” and it fits the textual inference from §1’s enumerated examples (seamen and railroad employees) that the exemption reaches workers who physically participate in the stream of interstate transportation even if they do not themselves cross state lines. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon, 596 U.S. 450 (2022), instructs that the inquiry is worker-focused and turns on whether the class of workers is directly involved in moving goods in interstate commerce; last-mile drivers can qualify when they transport goods still in that interstate journey. Petitioners’ proposed warehouse-based cutoff is not found in the statutory text and risks narrowing §1 beyond its original public meaning, though courts must apply the exemption with attention to administrability and precedent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FAA §1 exempts “contracts of employment” of “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon the court must identify the relevant “class of workers” by the “actual work” they perform and ask whether that work is part of interstate transportation, not whether the individual worker personally crosses state lines. Where last-mile drivers’ intrastate deliveries are a final leg of a continuous interstate movement of goods—i.e., the goods were shipped across state lines as part of an integrated journey to a predetermined endpoint—those drivers are engaged in interstate commerce for §1 purposes and are excluded from the FAA. A categorical rule that the interstate journey always ends at a warehouse is not compelled by the statutory text and risks underprotecting workers whose labor functionally completes interstate carriage, while a fact-sensitive inquiry better serves procedural fairness by aligning enforceability of arbitration clauses with the real nature of the transportation work. This approach also fits §1’s historically transportation-focused carveout, consistent with Circuit City’s instruction to read the residual clause narrowly but not artificially to require border-crossing by the worker.
